A.explanation: A gain of one up quark with no loss of down quarks would increase total quark number, which cannot happen when one quark simply changes flavour.

B.explanation: Beta-minus decay changes one down quark into one up quark, so up quarks increase by 1 and down quarks decrease by 1.

C.explanation: This describes the reverse change of up to down, which occurs in $\beta^+$ decay, not $\beta^-$ decay.

D.explanation: Down quarks do not increase in $\beta^-$ decay; one down quark is lost when it converts to an up quark.

hints: Notice the wording emits a $\beta^-$ particle - this means a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton.
Recall the quark make-up: a proton is $uud$ and a neutron is $udd$, so compare up and down counts before and after.
Count the change: one $d$ quark disappears and one $u$ quark appears, then match $+1$ and $-1$ to the up quarks and down quarks columns.
walkthrough: Identify the nucleon change: $\beta^-$ decay is $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, so one neutron becomes one proton inside the nucleus.
State the quark rule: proton composition is $uud$ with 2 up and 1 down, neutron composition is $udd$ with 1 up and 2 down.
Compare before and after for the single nucleon: up quarks go from 1 to 2, a change of $+1$, and down quarks go from 2 to 1, a change of $-1$.
Check the cause: at quark level one down quark changes flavour to an up quark, written $d \rightarrow u + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, so total quark number is conserved.
Match to the table: up quarks $+1$ with down quarks $-1$ corresponds to the row listed. This is option B
